results.title: Work Life Panda: Every task, every calendar, one app. ...
results.content:
Underneath it's a real task manager, and the AI that turns a sentence or your voice into a task runs on your device. Small local models, no cloud round-trip for the everyday stuff. "Private by default" isn't a tagline here.  
  
And then the bit nobody expects: every task and event carries its own chat, files and history. Share one into a private Family, Group or Work space and the conversation about a thing lives on the thing, instead of scrolling away in a group chat.  
  
It's early access and completely free while I build. No ads, no purchases yet. I'd genuinely love brutal feedback: what clicks, what's missing, and, if you'd ever pay for something like this, what would make it worth it. I'm in the comments all day. 🐼  
  
iPhone · iPad · Android · web. Links above. [...] 👋 Hey Product Hunt, I'm Andrea, the maker behind Work Life Panda.  
  
My week lived in a calendar, my to-dos in a list, and every plan involving another person in a group chat: three apps, none of which talked to each other. So I built the merge: a real task manager and a real calendar that are the same thing.  
  
And it starts full. Sign in with one tap, connect the calendar you already use (Google, Apple, Outlook or others) and your actual week is just there: still your calendar, not a copy, so a change in either place is a change in both. Connect a mailbox and the invitations already sitting in it quietly become events. Nothing to import, nothing to retype. [...] Work Life Panda

#### What's great

There is a moment in every workflow where you realise a tool is not just useful, it is foundational. Obsidian was that moment for me.

Before making the switch, I was living inside Apple Notes. It worked well enough for quick personal reminders and short captures, but the moment content got complex, the cracks showed. Formatting would break, structure was hard to maintain, and anything I wanted to reference later was buried somewhere with no real logic holding it together. For light personal use, Apple Notes is fine. For building a serious knowledge system, especially one designed to work alongside AI, it simply was not built for that job. [...] The graph view and visual thinking side of Obsidian also had a real effect on me. Seeing ideas connected in space changed the way I organize thoughts. It made planning feel less like filling boxes and more like building a living map of what I am working on.

Since I started using Obsidian, my productivity has gone up massively. I think more clearly, return to old ideas faster, and build long-term projects without losing context.

It has a learning curve, but that is also part of why it is powerful. Obsidian does not force a workflow on you. It gives you the raw material to build your own operating system for thinking. [...] #### What needs improvement

Search is the big one. It matches text, not meaning. If I remember the shape of a thought but not the words I used, there is no path from one to the other except scrolling. For a tool whose whole pitch is that it holds everything you know, not being able to ask it a fuzzy question is the gap I hit most often.

Second, the plugin situation cuts both ways. The ecosystem is genuinely why the tool is flexible, but a vault assembled from a dozen community plugins has a dozen independent maintainers and a dozen ways to break on an update. Some notion of a stable, supported core set would let people build on it with less anxiety.
